name: NCP1200D100R2G
title: Current-mode PWM controller for low-power, universal-input off-line supplies
summary: The NCP1200 is a fixed-frequency, peak current-mode PWM controller for small off-line flyback supplies such as wall adapters, battery chargers and standby supplies. It powers itself straight from the high-voltage rail through an internal current source, so no auxiliary winding is needed, and it drives an external MOSFET or IGBT. Light loads are handled by skipping cycles at a low, adjustable peak current, and an overload or open loop is caught by a timed latch-off that retries on its own. It comes in 40, 60 and 100 kHz versions in SOIC-8 and PDIP-8.

pins.name: Adj
pins.function: Sets the peak-current level at which cycle skipping begins. Left open it sits at 1.4 V behind a 25 kΩ source impedance; a resistor to ground lowers the level and a resistor to a higher voltage raises it.

pins.name: FB
pins.function: Feedback input. An optocoupler pulls this pin down against the internal 8 kΩ pull-up to set the peak current according to the load.

pins.name: CS
pins.function: Current sense input. Takes the voltage across the primary sense resistor and passes it, after leading-edge blanking, to the current comparator.

pins.name: Drv
pins.function: Gate drive output for the external MOSFET, ±250 mA peak.

pins.name: VCC
pins.function: Supply of the controller. Takes a bulk capacitor to ground, typically 10 µF, charged from HV by the internal current source.

pins.name: NC
pins.function: Not connected inside. Left empty to give creepage distance between HV and the low-voltage pins.

pins.name: HV
pins.function: High-voltage input. Ties to the rectified bulk rail and charges the VCC capacitor with a constant current during start-up and self-supply.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: An off-line flyback giving 6.5 V at 600 mA from a universal mains input. The mains passes an EMI filter and a bridge onto the 400 V bulk capacitor C3. The NCP1200 runs from that rail through its HV pin and a series resistor, with C5 holding VCC; it drives M1, which switches the transformer primary, and reads the switch current across Rsense. On the secondary, D2 and C2 rectify and smooth the output. The 5.1 V zener D8, the optocoupler LED and Rf set the regulation point: when the output passes the zener plus LED voltage, the phototransistor pulls FB down and lowers the peak current. Adj is left open, so skipping starts at the default level.

parts.note: series resistor in the HV lead; the HV-pin protection calls for more than 4.7 kΩ.
P2 (drain end) and S1 (anode end) are the dotted ends

circuits.title: 3.5 W AC-DC wall adapter
circuits.description: A complete 6.5 V, 600 mA wall adapter for a load that has its own regulator. R9 sits in series with one mains line. After the bridge, C3, L5 and C2 form a pi filter on the bulk rail, with L6 in the return and a resistor across each inductor. The NCP1200 runs from the bulk rail through HV with C9 on VCC, drives M1 and senses its current in R6. An RCD clamp across the primary (Rclamp, Cclamp, Dclamp) and an RC snubber at the drain are both optional. On the secondary, D3 rectifies into C5, and L4 with C10 filters the ripple before the output. R2, the optocoupler IC1 and the 5.1 V zener D6 close the loop onto FB. The short-circuit protection is internal.

circuits.title: HV pin fed through a diode from one mains line
circuits.description: The HV pin takes its current through the 1N4007 Dstart from one AC line after the EMI filter instead of from the bulk rail. The pin then sees a half-wave rectified voltage averaging 2·Vmains,peak/π, which cuts the power the self-supply burns inside the controller.
notes: The ground and lower bulk connections run on to the rest of the converter.

circuits.title: Series resistor in the HV lead
circuits.description: A resistor of more than 4.7 kΩ between the bulk capacitor and HV limits the current that flows out of the pin if the bulk node rings below ground at switch-off, so the internal parasitic SCR does not latch and dump CVCC through the chip.
notes: The other pins connect as in the typical application.

circuits.title: Diode from VCC to the bulk capacitor
circuits.description: A 1N4007 with its anode on VCC and its cathode on the bulk rail and HV. As the bulk voltage collapses at switch-off it pulls VCC down with it, so VCC reaches the undervoltage threshold and switching stops before the bulk capacitor is deeply discharged. Two diodes in series may be used for margin.
notes: The other pins connect as in the typical application.

circuits.title: Faster turn-on and turn-off
circuits.description: A complementary emitter follower, 2N2222 above and 2N2907 below, buffers Drv to the MOSFET gate and speeds both edges. Rd in series with the bases damps overshoot from long traces and can be left out when the connections are short. The VCC capacitor also supplies the NPN collector.

parts.note: damping; can be left out when the wiring is short

notes: The other pins connect as in the typical application.
With a standard 2N2222/2N2907 pair the rise and fall times improved about five times.

circuits.title: Faster turn-off only
circuits.description: Drv charges the gate through a 1N4148. At turn-off Drv falls, the 2N2907's base follows it and its emitter pulls the gate down hard, so only the falling edge is speeded up.
notes: The other pins connect as in the typical application.

circuits.title: Faster turn-on only
circuits.description: A 2N2222 follower from VCC charges the gate when Drv rises. At turn-off the gate discharges into Drv through a 1N4148, so the falling edge stays as the chip makes it.
notes: The other pins connect as in the typical application.

operation.text: The oscillator is fixed inside the chip at 40, 60 or 100 kHz, chosen by part number, and carries a built-in frequency jitter that spreads the EMI. The SOIC-8 is marked 200D followed by 4, 6 or 1 for 40, 60 or 100 kHz; the PDIP-8 is marked 1200P followed by 40, 60 or 100. All versions are lead-free, halogen-free and RoHS compliant. The part is marked discontinued and not for new designs.

Peak current mode: each cycle the clock sets the latch and the drive goes high; it goes low when the CS voltage, after a leading-edge blanking time of 230 ns typical, reaches the setpoint from FB. FB has an 8 kΩ internal pull-up, the setpoint on CS is the FB voltage divided by 4, and the peak current can never exceed 1 V / Rsense. Maximum duty cycle is 80 %. Timing parts, feedback amplifier, filtering and start-up are all inside, so the converter needs no auxiliary winding.

A current source of about 4 mA from HV charges the VCC capacitor. At power-on it runs with no output pulses until VCC reaches VCCOFF (11.4 V typical); it then turns off and the chip switches from the stored charge. When VCC falls to VCCON (9.8 V typical) the source turns back on while pulses continue, so VCC ramps between the two levels, averaging about 10.6 V with a 10 µF capacitor. The loss in this source grows with the HV voltage and the gate charge.

Three ways to lower the standby loss: use a MOSFET with less gate charge; feed HV through a diode (typically 1N4007) from one mains line so it sees a half-wave average rather than the peak; or hold VCC above VCCOFF from an auxiliary winding, which keeps the HV source permanently off. An auxiliary winding must never take VCC past 16 V.

As the load falls, the loop lowers the peak current through FB. When FB reaches the skip level (1.4 V by default, set by Adj) the peak current stops falling and the controller blanks whole switching cycles instead, delivering energy in bursts whose width follows the load. Skipping happens at a low peak current (350 mV / Rsense by default), so the transformer makes no audible noise. Above 1.4 V on FB the part runs in normal current mode; below it, in skip mode. The skip level can be lowered by a resistor from Adj to ground or raised by a resistor from Adj to a higher voltage.

On self-supply the chip dissipates the HV voltage less 11 V times its consumption, which on a 350 V DC rail with the 100 kHz version exceeds what a PDIP-8 at 100 °C/W can shed at 70 °C ambient. 80 mm² of 1 oz (35 µm) copper round the PDIP-8 lowers RθJA to about 75 °C/W, enough for the 100 kHz version. The SOIC-8 is 178 °C/W bare; a 12 mm × 12 mm pad of 1 oz copper, or 6.5 mm × 6.5 mm of 2 oz (70 µm), brings it to 100 °C/W. The 100 kHz SOIC-8 is not recommended with the self-supply active unless that copper area is available; a diode in series with HV (dropping the average to 222 V and the dissipation below 400 mW) or an auxiliary winding removes the restriction. Thermal shutdown is at 140 °C typical.

A shorted output, or a broken optocoupler, leaves no current in the opto LED, so FB rises to its internal 4.1 V and the peak current goes to the maximum. The chip watches for this overload whenever VCC falls from VCCOFF: if the overload is still present when VCC reaches VCCON, it stops driving, keeps the HV source off and drops to 350 µA (ICC3). VCC then sinks slowly to the latch-off end level (6.3 V typical), where a new start-up begins: the source recharges VCC to 11.4 V and pulses resume. If the fault has gone the converter carries on; otherwise the cycle repeats, giving a low-duty burst until the fault clears. During start-up the peak current also sits at the maximum until the output reaches regulation.

The time VCC takes to fall from 11.4 V to 9.8 V must be longer than the time the converter needs to bring its output into regulation at full load, or the start-up is taken for an overload and the supply never starts. Measure or simulate the start-up time, choose a fall time with margin (10 ms for a 6 ms start-up) and size the capacitor from the consumption including gate drive.

Being a CMOS part, the controller can be latched by negative voltages on its pins, which forward-bias the substrate and can fire internal parasitic SCRs; with a low-impedance path from VCC to GND the stored charge in the VCC capacitor then destroys the chip. CS is the usual victim, but HV is also at risk at switch-off: the converter keeps switching from the VCC capacitor, and if the network of Lp and the bulk capacitor has a low Q the bulk node can ring below ground. The bridge clamps the bulk node to about −2 Vf. A resistor of more than 4.7 kΩ in series with HV, or a diode from VCC to the bulk capacitor so VCC reaches the undervoltage threshold early, prevents the latch-up.

The output stage is asymmetric to soften the EMI: it sources through about 40 Ω and sinks through about 12 Ω, so the MOSFET turns on slowly and off fast. One or two bipolar transistors added at the output speed the turn-on, the turn-off or both.

With low leakage inductance the MTD1N60E can absorb occasional avalanche energy, such as a mains surge, unaided. If the leakage spike drives the drain above the MOSFET's 600 V BVdss in normal running, an RCD clamp (Rclamp, Cclamp, Dclamp) is required; the clamp diode must be very fast, a MUR160 type. An RC snubber across the drain is the alternative: it damps the leakage ringing and adds capacitance at turn-off; 1.5 kΩ and 47 pF are typical starting values in a 4 W design, to be trimmed for dissipation against standby power.

The 3.5 W, 6.5 V adapter serves loads such as toys, calculators and CD players that regulate internally and need only a raw DC level; the controller's built-in short-circuit protection keeps the parts count low.
